title: The bee (I.3)
hookLine: devotion suits every vocation, like a bee takes honey without harming the flower
tomorrow: do you need a guide, or is God enough?

lines: A NEW HABIT CAN WRECK A LIFE.
THREE PEOPLE TRYING TO BE HOLY.
cards: A new habit can wreck a life. The morning workout that makes you late for everyone else, the diet the whole house has to eat. So how do you add something to a life without wrecking it?
Francis de Sales has a strange answer.

In chapter three he lists three people trying hard to be holy: a bishop who lives alone in silence like a monk, a married person who wants to own nothing like a friar, a worker who stays in church all day.
And he calls all three ridiculous. Why would a saint say that?

teach.b: Because their devotion doesn't fit their lives. At creation, de Sales recalls, God told the plants to bear fruit each after its kind.

In the same way, he says, devotion is meant to be lived by each person according to their state: the worker, the servant, the ruler, the widow, the young, the married. The bishop has a diocese to care for.
The married person has a household. The worker has work that's going undone.

teach.h: DEVOTION THAT WRECKS IS OUT OF ORDER.
teach.b: Devotion that wrecks a calling is out of order. Then the picture that solves the puzzle.

teach.h: THE BEE LEAVES THE FLOWER WHOLE.
teach.b: He borrows a line he credits to Aristotle: the bee takes honey from flowers without harming them, and leaves them as whole and fresh as it found them. True devotion, de Sales says, does even better. It spoils no calling.
It makes each one more beautiful.
Here's one for tonight: he says precious stones dipped in honey shine brighter, each in its own color. So the answer to the hook: add devotion the way a bee visits a flower.
If the family, the team or the job is worse off, something's out of order.

how: Catholics speak of holiness in one's state of life: married people, workers, students, priests and religious each live devotion in a different way, a theme the Church took up strongly in the Second Vatican Council's universal call to holiness.

o: a honey offering left at a shrine on feast days
devotion that fits your life and harms none of it
a busy person who never takes time to pray

p: devotion fits each state of life
a bishop living like a monk
takes honey, leaves the flower whole
shine brighter, each in its color

s: the holiest devotion is the most time spent in church
de Sales calls a worker who stays in church while the work goes undone out of order.
de Sales says true devotion makes every calling more beautiful
like stones dipped in honey, each shines in its own color.
de Sales says devotion is the same for a bishop and a parent
each after its kind: it fits each state of life differently.

games.q: a new dad wants to pray an hour every night, but it means his wife does every bedtime alone. what would de Sales say?
o: find devotion that fits the household, so it isn't worse off.
keep the full hour; prayer comes before everything else.
give up prayer for now; family life leaves no room for it.
games.why: devotion that wrecks a calling is out of order. the bee takes honey and leaves the flower whole, and better.

practice: Pick one small task you'll do today, a shift, a set of dishes, a homework problem, a diaper. Picture doing it slowly and well, leaving the people around it better off than you found them.
Then do one tiny piece of it with that care right now, even straightening one thing within reach.

wordCard.voice: The bee. De Sales's picture of devotion: it draws honey from every calling and harms none, leaving each one brighter.

carryVoice: Carry this: honey without harm, devotion that leaves the flower whole and the work brighter. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Introduction to the Devout Life I.3
